title: Smart Toilets Are Already Using AI to Analyze Your Poop
gist: AI-powered stool-tracking toilet attachments from Kohler Health and the venture-backed startup Throne are chasing a nearly $106 billion gut-health market via hardware-plus-subscription pricing, but gastroenterologists question their clinical value for healthy users and their real-world viability as cheap enough cancer-screening tools, while privacy advocates flag subscription lock-in on sensitive health data.

insights.claim: The global gut-health market is projected to reach nearly $106 billion by 2029, the backdrop driving multiple companies including Kohler Health and Throne into AI-powered stool-analysis toilet attachments.
insights.speaker: Gabriela Galvin
insights.so_what: Quantifies a large adjacent digital-health market that toilet-based biosensing products are trying to capture a slice of.

insights.claim: Kohler Health, an offshoot of the plumbing giant Kohler, prices its stool tracker at $449 plus a $130 annual family membership; Throne, a startup that raised $10 million in July, prices its device at $399 plus a $70 annual membership.
insights.speaker: Gabriela Galvin
insights.so_what: A classic hardware-plus-recurring-subscription health-tech model; the $10M raise is an early-stage funding data point, and gating access to one's own health data behind a subscription is a business-model and regulatory risk area with precedent in the 23andMe-style backlash.
insights.locator: paragraph introducing Kohler Health and Throne pricing

insights.claim: A gastroenterologist and spokesperson for the American Gastroenterological Association argues that for healthy people with regular bowel movements, AI stool analysis offers little new insight since users could simply look at their own stool, calling the tech 'overkill.'
insights.speaker: Gabriela Galvin
insights.so_what: Signals thin near-term clinical differentiation for the mass-market wellness segment versus marketing claims, a key skepticism point for evaluating the addressable market size.
insights.quote: It kind of seems like overkill. If you want to look at your stool, you can just look at it yourself. I don't know that the AI is bringing a lot of new science to this.

insights.claim: Throne's roadmap includes a next-generation device using multispectral imaging, far more sensitive than the naked eye, to detect blood in stool as an early colorectal-cancer screening signal; a prototype has shown promising early results and the company expects to launch the updated device within about two years, with pricing not yet determined.
insights.speaker: Gabriela Galvin
insights.so_what: A longer-horizon bet on becoming a low-cost cancer-screening adjunct; colorectal cancer is now the leading cause of cancer death among people under 50 per the article, giving the roadmap real addressable urgency if it pans out, though unproven and not yet clinically validated.
insights.locator: paragraphs on Throne's multispectral imaging roadmap

insights.claim: An independent gastroenterology professor at the Catholic University of Rome argues that even if blood-detection technology proves clinically meaningful, these devices remain too expensive to serve as viable population-level cancer screening tools, since effective screening tests must be both non-invasive and cheap.
insights.speaker: Gabriela Galvin
insights.so_what: Articulates the core commercial tension for consumer health-hardware startups seeking medical-device-style positioning: pricing must fall dramatically to unlock screening-scale volume and reimbursement potential.
insights.quote: A screening test should be non-invasive but also cheap—and this is not cheap.

insights.claim: Colorectal cancer has become the leading cause of cancer death among people under 50, with rising rates over the past decade whose cause is unclear, though ultra-processed food, microplastics, and antibiotics exposure are suspected contributors.
insights.speaker: Gabriela Galvin
insights.so_what: Establishes the underlying public-health trend that gives stool-monitoring products genuine addressable urgency beyond wellness-optimization hype.

insights.claim: Both companies collect standard personal data such as name and demographics plus intimate biometric stool/urine data; Kohler Health additionally tracks users' precise location while Throne does not, a specific privacy-exposure differentiator between the two competitors.
insights.speaker: Gabriela Galvin
insights.so_what: A concrete data point for comparing privacy risk profiles between the two direct competitors in this emerging category.

insights.claim: Both companies state they don't sell user health data for targeted advertising, but their privacy policies allow sharing data with law enforcement, an acquiring company in a merger or sale, and third-party service providers, a risk flagged by a Mozilla Foundation digital-rights advocate given how re-upped long-term subscriptions make it psychologically harder for users to walk away from accumulated personal health data.
insights.speaker: Gabriela Galvin
insights.so_what: An underappreciated risk vector for consumer health-hardware subscriptions, especially relevant given the sensitivity of the data and possible future acquisition or bankruptcy scenarios exposing it.
insights.locator: paragraphs on data sharing and subscription lock-in
